Chart B — Scoring more vs stopping goals: which pays faster?

Scoring changeGoals-allowed change
How to read this chart —

Left is 15% worse than last season, right is 15% better, centre is baseline. Both lines climb steadily (~3½–4 points per 5% step) with no sudden cliff. The green line finishes slightly higher: preventing goals pays a little more than scoring them. Cases S1 and S2.

04 · Method & Test

Four steps, one frozen test.

If you can explain it, you can trust it. A direct formula check agrees with the simulation within 0.35 points on every case.

1

Measure

82 real games → 3.26 scored / 2.61 allowed per 60 min; tied games split 12–12.

2

Draw scores

Goals drawn at random around those averages — the standard model for rare events.

3

Simulate 10,000×

Full 82-game seasons, fixed seed 3315, so anyone reproduces identical results.

4

Change one thing

Then replay. Players credited only for games they actually missed — no double-counting.

Backtest

106 predicted → 112 actual

Built only from 2024–25, frozen, aimed at 2025–26: error 6.1 pts, inside the likely range, wins exact (50). Nothing re-tuned. One test is evidence, not proof — stated openly.

Quality

30/30 checks · tests pass

188 source files saved with fingerprints. Two QA-found mistakes fixed, re-tested and documented. NHL official data [1–6], Hockey-Reference cross-check [7–9].

Limits

What it cannot see

Average opponents only · injuries/trades/schedules averaged out · tied-game rate from one season · Central view from 2021–22 → 2025–26.

Reproducible by design

Fully reproducible —

The complete analysis is open and reproducible from the project repository: the data checks, model configuration, and automated tests are all included. Every case was simulated over 10,000 seasons using a fixed random seed (3315), so the same inputs produce the same results. If the underlying collected data changes, the forecasts may change with it — that is expected, and the repository records exactly which data was used.
